ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The attached diagram shows three cords meeting at a single junction. A horizontal cord extends left from the junction and is labeled T = 10 N. A vertical cord extends downward from the junction to a hanging mass labeled W = ?. A slanted cord extends upward-right from the junction to the ceiling, and the angle between this slanted cord and the horizontal ceiling is marked 60°. Reasoning: Consider the forces at the junction in static equilibrium. Let the tension in the slanted cord be S. The left horizontal cord pulls with 10 N, so horizontal balance gives S cos 60° = 10. The vertical cord supports the mass, so vertical balance gives S sin 60° = W. Dividing the vertical equation by the horizontal equation gives W/10 = tan 60° = √3. Therefore W = 10√3 N.

method.method_draft: First read the diagram: at the junction there are exactly three concurrent tensions: 10 N horizontally to the left, W vertically downward through the hanging mass, and an unknown slanted tension along a cord that is 60° above the horizontal. Construct the force triangle for equilibrium: the horizontal 10 N force and vertical W force are perpendicular legs, and their resultant must be exactly opposite the slanted cord. Since the slanted cord is 60° above the horizontal, the resultant of the 10 N horizontal and W vertical components has slope tan 60° = W/10. Therefore W = 10 tan 60° = 10√3 N.
